## The factors that move the number

**Area and layout.** A single flat accent wall is a fundamentally different
job from a stairwell, a room with many windows and doors, or a space with
curved or sloped surfaces. Cuts around obstacles take far longer per square
foot than open wall does, so two rooms of identical size can differ
substantially.

## Why preparation matters more than people expect

A wallcovering follows the surface underneath it. Anything left on the wall —
a lump, a seam, a patch of loose paint, a ridge of old adhesive — shows
through the finished result, sometimes more visibly than it did before. Most
finishes that disappoint were installed over a surface that was not ready,
not hung badly.

## What preparation typically involves

## What preparation typically involves

**Removing existing covering.** Difficulty varies enormously. Modern
strippable papers can come away cleanly in whole lengths. Older layers,
painted-over wallpaper, or covering applied directly to unsealed drywall can
be slow and can damage the surface as it comes off, creating repair work that
was not visible beforehand. This is the single hardest part of a job to
predict without seeing it.

was not visible beforehand. This is the single hardest part of a job to

**Repairing the substrate.** Filling holes and cracks, re-fixing loose areas,
addressing any damp — which needs the cause fixed, not just the symptom, since
moisture will lift a new covering as readily as it lifted the old one.

**Dealing with texture.** Heavily textured surfaces generally need skimming
flat. This is a plastering operation with its own drying time.

**Sealing or priming.** Bare or porous surfaces are usually sealed so that
adhesive behaves predictably and so the covering can be removed cleanly in
future without destroying the wall underneath.

## Newly built or freshly plastered walls

New plaster needs to dry fully and is normally sealed before covering. Hanging
over plaster that has not finished drying tends to fail.

How residential and commercial wallcovering work differ — Both are wallcovering, but they are run differently, and the differences
explain why the two are usually quoted and scheduled separately.

## Residential

Usually one room or one wall, chosen for how it will look and feel. The
decision is personal and often aesthetic before it is practical: a bedroom
that should feel calm, a dining room that should feel like an occasion, a
hallway that is the first thing anyone sees.

Practical characteristics: the space is occupied, so furniture protection and
tidiness matter as much as the finish; work is measured in days; and the
client is normally present and involved in choosing the material.

Durability requirements are modest in most rooms. Bathrooms, kitchens and
children's rooms are the exceptions, where moisture and cleaning matter.

## Commercial

Offices, hotels, restaurants, retail, healthcare, common areas of residential
buildings. Larger areas, and driven by different priorities.

**Regulation can apply.** Commercial interiors are often subject to fire

Types of wallcovering material — General background on the main families of wallcovering and what each is
suited to. Which of these any particular company offers is a separate
question.

## Non-woven

The most common modern substrate. A blend of natural and synthetic fibres that
is dimensionally stable, meaning it does not expand when it gets wet and does
not shrink as it dries. Usually hung by pasting the wall rather than the
material, which is faster and cleaner, and it is normally strippable in one
piece later. A sensible default for most residential rooms.

## Vinyl

A printed backing with a vinyl surface. Wipeable, hard-wearing, tolerant of
moisture. Contract-grade vinyls are the standard choice for commercial and
high-traffic settings, and are manufactured to defined durability and fire
performance classes. Heavier and less breathable than paper, which matters on
walls prone to damp.

## Traditional paper

Printed paper, sometimes with a decorative coating. Often the best reproduction
of historical and hand-blocked designs, and favoured in period settings. Less
tolerant of moisture and handling than the alternatives, and expands when
pasted, so it demands more skill to hang well.

## Natural fibre — grasscloth, sisal, silk

Woven natural material on a paper backing. Texture and depth that printed
finishes cannot reproduce. Two properties matter and are often not explained
to clients beforehand: seams are visible by nature, since a natural fibre
cannot be pattern-matched, and colour varies between rolls. Both are inherent
to the material rather than defects. Not suited to humid rooms or heavy
contact.

An image printed to the dimensions of one specific wall and supplied as
numbered panels. Anything can be produced — a photograph, artwork, a scaled
pattern. Because it is made for one wall it must be measured precisely before
printing, and a change afterwards means reprinting rather than reordering.

Where the wall is and what happens to it — moisture, contact, cleaning; how the
